title: Architecture & Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance, and ADR Process
author: Sofia Martinez
body:
Summary

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's cross-cutting architecture and engineering standards: API design, coding conventions, infrastructure (cloud & on-prem), model-serving best practices, observability standards, performance targets, and the Decision Record (ADR) process. It is intended for engineers, tech leads, product managers, and SREs as the canonical reference for design decisions and runtime expectations.

Scope

Applies to all services and components that participate in inference delivery: hosted API backend, routing and smart routing services, serving runtime, model compilation/kernels, Dedicated and Private deployment packaging, and platform telemetry. Does NOT replace team-specific runbooks or tactical implementation details; it sets company-wide minimums and patterns.

Standards (high level)

1) API Standards
- Use REST+JSON for public-facing control-plane APIs and RPC/gRPC for high-throughput internal transport between services where low latency and strong typing are required.
- API Versioning: mount versions in the URI: /v1/, /v2/. Backwards-incompatible changes require an ADR and a deprecation plan (90 days minimum for internal clients, 180 days for external customers).
- Request/response contracts: use documented JSON Schema files in the repo (schemas/api/) and publish bundles to the API docs site. All POST/PUT endpoints must validate against the canonical schema.
- Error model: adopt structured errors: {"code": string, "message": string, "details": optional object}. Map internal HTTP codes to customer-facing codes in an errors.md reference.
- Authentication: all external APIs require token-based auth (Bearer + scoped API keys). Service-to-service calls use mTLS or short-lived JWTs (see infra standards).
- Rate limiting and quotas: default per-tenant rate limit is 20 rps; endpoints that accept tokenized workloads (generation) should expose token accounting headers (X-Redwood-Tokens-Consumed).
- SDK contracts: SDKs must only depend on stable endpoints and respect back-off headers. Changes to SDK-visible behavior must follow SDK release guidance.

2) Coding Standards
- Languages: Go for infra & gateway services; Python for evaluation and orchestration scripts; Rust/C++ only for performance-critical runtime kernels with documented FFI boundaries.
- Style & linting: enforce gofmt/golangci-lint, black + ruff for Python, clang-format for C++/Rust style guidelines. CI must fail on lint regressions.
- Testing: unit tests >= 75% coverage for new modules; integration tests for cross-service flows; fuzz tests for parser/decoder code in runtimes.
- Dependency policy: no direct dependency on internet-hosted artifacts at build time for release artifacts. All external binaries must be pinned and checksummed in third_party/ or fetched through approved package manifests.
- Feature flags: all non-trivial behavioral changes controlled via the feature-flag service; default to safe/off state and require rollout/kill-switch documentation.
- Code ownership: each repository must list at least two code owners in CODEOWNERS; critical libraries must have explicit oncall rotation.

3) Infrastructure Standards
- Network: VPC-per-environment (dev/staging/prod). Production control plane and customer data plane network segmentation enforced with NACLs and security groups.
- Identity: single source of truth for identities is the internal IAM; integrate IAM groups to role-based access. Long-lived keys disallowed in production; use ephemeral credentials and KMS.
- Secrets: all secrets stored in the company KMS (AWS KMS / GCP KMS or HSM for on-prem) and referenced via environment variable injection at runtime. No plaintext secrets in source.
- Provisioning: Terraform for cloud IAC with state locking; on-prem packaging uses the reference-architectures/* manifests. Pull requests that change Terraform must include a plan output and cost delta estimation.
- Observability ingress: all production hosts must ship logs, metrics, and traces to the platform observability cluster using the standardized agent and schema.

4) Model-serving Standards
- Model artifact layouts: require VCS-friendly model manifests (model.yaml) including model_id, version, architecture, quantization_profile, compatible_kernels, max_context_tokens, memory_profile. Example:

```yaml
model_id: redwood-13b-v1
version: 2026-03-01
architecture: transformer
quantization_profile: q4_0
compatible_kernels: [cuda-faster-attn, cpu-avx2]
max_context_tokens: 8192
memory_profile: high
```

- Kernel & compilation policy: runtime teams maintain canonical kernel selection logic. New kernel integrations must provide benchmark artifacts (p95 latency, throughput curves, memory footprint) and a compatibility ADR.
- KV cache and caching policy: prefix caching enabled by default for high-reuse workloads; cache keys must be namespaced by tenant + model_id + model_version + prompt_fingerprint. Cache TTL default 24h; shorter for private deployments where customer policy mandates.
- Quantization: follow quantization-profiles/ guidelines. Acceptable default for Dedicated is q4_0 or q8_0; any lower-bit profiles require evaluation for quality regressions and an ADR describing tradeoffs.
- Warmup & preloading: models must provide a warmup script (warmup.sh) that executes representative inference calls to prime kernels and memory allocators. Deployment orchestrator will run warmup in the prestart hook.

5) Observability Standards
- Traces: trace every external request from ingress to model invocation and response emission. Use OpenTelemetry semantic conventions. Include baggage fields: tenant_id, request_id, route, model_id, model_version.
- Metrics: standardized metric names with tags; minimal SLI set for inference routes: inference_requests_total, inference_errors_total, inference_latency_ms_bucket (histogram), tokens_generated_total, batch_size_distribution.
- Logs: structured JSON logs with keys: ts, level, service, request_id, tenant_id, component, message. No PII in logs. Sensitive payloads must be redacted by middleware.
- Dashboards & alerts: each service must publish a per-route dashboard (latency, error rate, RPS, tokens). Alert thresholds (see performance section).

6) Performance Standards (SLOs & thresholds)
- Company default SLOs for user-facing inference endpoints (applies to hosted and Dedicated with SLA):
  - Availability: 99.95% monthly for paid production routes.
  - Latency (p95): <= 500ms for short-context (<=512 tokens) gen requests; p95 <= 1200ms for long-context (>=2048 tokens).
  - Error rate (5xx): <= 0.2% (0.002) over rolling 30-day window.
- Cost-performance guidance: target tokens/sec per GPU metrics for common instance types documented in benchmarking-and-perf-suite. Include expected batch-size profiles.
- Capacity planning: SRE to maintain 30% spare headroom in production GPU pools during business hours; autoscaling policies must maintain recovery within 3 minutes of traffic surge to avoid SLA breaches.

Decision Records (ADRs) Process

Purpose: ADRs capture architectural decisions that materially affect system behavior, costs, security, or operations.

When to write an ADR:
1. Introducing a new cross-team runtime kernel or hardware type.
2. Making breaking or irreversible API contract changes.
3. Changing global operational practices (e.g., encryption at rest approach, multi-region topology).
4. Any decision that changes SLO targets or billing model.

ADR template (file in docs/adr/):
- Title: short, descriptive
- Status: proposed | accepted | superseded | deprecated
- Context: background and constraints
- Decision: concrete chosen approach
- Consequences: operational, cost, and migration implications
- Owners and review list
- Date and links to related benchmarks or tickets

Process steps (numbered):
1. Draft ADR in the ADR repo under docs/adr/YYYY-MM-DD-title.md.
2. Assign at least two reviewers from affected teams.
3. Run a 5-business-day asynchronous review; capture objections and mitigation steps.
4. If accepted, move status to accepted, communicate on #architecture and send to product & SRE mailing list.
5. If the ADR implies code changes, create a companion PR with tests, rollout plan, and a rollback procedure.
6. Maintain a single source of truth list (docs/adr/index.md) and reference ADR id in related code repos.

Enforcement and Governance
- CI gates: PRs that change API schemas, Terraform provisioning, or runtime kernel bindings must include: schema diff, terraform plan output, and benchmark artifacts respectively. CI will run schema linter and basic integration tests.
- Architecture Council: a standing panel (representatives from Runtime, SRE, Platform, Security, Product) reviews ADRs that touch cross-cutting concerns or exceed a defined cost threshold (> $10k/month).
- Audits: quarterly architecture audits to validate adherence to standards and identify drift; results published to the architecture-and-standards audits page.

Appendix: Example configs and checks

1) Example API error response (JSON):

{
  "code": "RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED",
  "message": "Rate limit exceeded for tenant",
  "details": { "limit": "20 rps", "window": "1s" }
}

2) Example warmup.sh snippet for model preloading:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
# warmup: run three representative requests to prime kernels
curl -s -X POST $WARMUP_ENDPOINT -H "Authorization: Bearer $WARMUP_TOKEN" -d '{"prompt":"Hello world","max_tokens":16}'
curl -s -X POST $WARMUP_ENDPOINT -H "Authorization: Bearer $WARMUP_TOKEN" -d '{"prompt":"Summarize: Redwood Inference","max_tokens":64}'
```

3) Terraform PR checklist snippet (to include in repo CONTRIBUTING.md):
- [ ] terraform plan included and warnings explained
- [ ] cost delta estimate included
- [ ] security review for open ports
- [ ] automated destroy acceptance test run (staging only)

Frequently Asked Questions
- Q: What if a team needs a temporary deviation from a standard?
  A: Draft an ADR titled "Temporary deviation: <short reason>" with a TTL (max 90 days) and an explicit rollback plan. The Architecture Council will review urgent short-lived deviations within 2 business days.

- Q: How are SLOs adjusted for Dedicated/Private deployments?
  A: Dedicated contracts may set custom SLOs in the SLA. Private on-prem deployments default to customer-managed SLOs; Redwood provides recommended SLO templates and tooling to measure them. Any change to default company SLOs must go through an ADR.
